newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe must reverse unpopularity to win French poll.
newsitem.headline: Juppe must reverse unpopularity to win French poll.

text.p: Alain Juppe, the least popular prime minister in modern French history, faces the daunting task of trying to become the first sitting premier to win re-election since 1978.

Juppe, seen as a brilliant but unfeeling technocrat, became the centre-right's champion and the left's number one target when President Jacques Chirac on Monday called a snap parliamentary election for May 25 and June 1.

In a 1993 speech to his Gaullist party, Chirac called Juppe "the best of us". But among voters, Juppe's popularity slumped last year to the lowest of any premier since the start of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
It has recovered only slightly since then, and only about 30 percent of voters now express confidence in him.

Juppe, 51, once grumbled that politicians and journalists looked at him "the way people watched a bullfight, waiting for the bull to be killed". In a book he wrote in 1993, he said he felt tempted to flee the vagaries of politics and retreat to Venice as a monk.
Six months ago, many coalition backbenchers would happily have bought him the plane ticket. But now the election campaign will force them to rally behind him.
Often blamed for problems ranging from record unemployment to austerity measures designed to qualify France for a single European currency, Juppe has a lot of ground to make up in the coming weeks.
No French prime minister has led his party to victory in National Assembly elections since Raymond Barre in 1978.

But Juppe, who came to office in May 1995 when Chirac won the presidency, can point to his courage in setting France on the painful but necessary track of reform and modernisation, though the price has been deep unpopularity.
He also starts the campaign with a giant outgoing majority, the ruling coalition holding 464 out of 577 National Assembly seats.

Bruised but defiant, Juppe has confounded critics who have forecast his political demise, especially after a crippling 24-day wave of labour unrest in 1995 triggered by his drive to rein in France's free-spending welfare system.
At the time, cartoonists portrayed his bald, domed head as a setting sun. But he is still there and the core of his health reforms -- higher taxes and spending curbs -- are in place.

"I would prefer to be loved than not to be loved, but I am not complaining," said Juppe when his popularity ratings hit rock bottom. Juppe, who entered politics as a speechwriter for Chirac in 1976, has retained his boss's unfailing support.

He has repeatedly tried to project a more human image to counter criticisms that he is abrasive and domineering in enforcing fiscal austerity to equip France for membership of the EU single currency from 1999.

Last year, he published a slim book baring his wounded soul in what he said was a move inspired by a woman who yelled abuse at him in the streets of Bordeaux, where he is mayor. Critics called it a tacky publicity stunt.
While Juppe remains unpopular, his main challenger, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, is considered lacking in charisma.
A highly respected foreign minister in 1993-95, Juppe became prime minister with stellar popularity ratings.
But his -- and Chirac's -- honeymoon with the voters fizzled out within months when they made an about-face on campaign pledges to cut unemployment and heal social divisions.

Juppe's image also suffered when it emerged, only a month after he took office, that he had obtained luxury city-owned apartments for himself and family members at below-market rents when he was an aide to Chirac, formerly Paris mayor.

Juppe escaped prosecution after promising to move out and suffered only a reprimand. He moved to the prime minister's residence with his second wife and infant daughter, who have played a prominent role in photo opportunities designed to "humanise" his image.
